interest: For historians of Japanese American history, transpacific migration, and interwar U.S.–Japan relations, this file is exceptional because it captures the voices, demographic data, and daily realities of Nisei who navigated life in Japan rather than the United States. Rather than relying solely on high-level diplomatic assessments, the file preserves rare institutional prospectuses, questionnaires, survey tabulations, and local press accounts illustrating specific Nisei cultural and economic niches—ranging from female jazz performers and English-language samurai theater to young Californians training in chick sexing for the U.S. poultry industry. Furthermore, it offers valuable insight into how U.S. diplomatic, labor, and military officials, alongside the Japanese government, monitored the loyalties, civil status, and potential propaganda value of dual-citizen youth on the eve of World War II.
overview: This file (State Department decimal file 894.42711) documents the social, economic, educational, and political conditions of second-generation Japanese Americans (Nisei) living, studying, and working in Japan during the mid-1930s. Anchored by an extensive September 1935 voluntary consular report prepared by U.S. Consul Richard F. Boyce in Yokohama and accompanied by diplomatic memoranda, interdepartmental correspondence (involving the State, Labor, and War Departments), and Japanese press clippings, the records analyze the drivers behind Nisei migration—most notably the Great Depression and favorable currency exchange rates. The file compiles rich primary documentation on the cultural alienation and linguistic hurdles facing these American citizens, institutional responses such as preparatory schools and dormitories (including the School for Foreign-Born Japanese, Waseda International Institute, and Kaigai Kyoiku Kyokai), Tokyo YMCA/YWCA demographic surveys, and governmental scrutiny over questions of dual nationality, national allegiance, and Japanese cultural propaganda.
